newsitem.title: DUBAI: Oman, Qatar business take slow steps with Israel.
newsitem.headline: Oman, Qatar business take slow steps with Israel.

text.p: Oman and Qatar have gone further than their Gulf Arab allies to establish ties with Israel, but businessmen in the oil states say trade flows are still low and some are still wary of dealing openly with the Jewish state.

Since Israeli trade missions were set up in Doha and Muscat earlier this year, business interest has been stoked, but joint venture investment and trade are yet to come, businessmen, bankers and traders told Reuters on Wednesday.

"There has not been much trading, at least we haven't seen any transactions through the banks," said an Omani banker, adding: "But any relationship takes time to develop. Since the trade offices have opened, as time passes we expect business."
"So far no concrete joint venture between Qatari and Israeli investors has emerged, but our work is going on," said Sammy Ravel, head of Israel's trade office in Qatar.

Even though the two Gulf states have stopped short of full diplomatic relations with Israel, Oman's trade office in Tel Aviv and Qatar's plans to open one there are a departure from general Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) policy.
The six GCC states say they will consider establishing diplomatic ties with Israel only when a just and comprehensive peace is reached, including on the Syrian and Lebanese tracks.

Of the Gulf states, Oman, Qatar, Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates have said they are sending delegations to next week's Middle East economic conference in Cairo, which was originally intended to integrate Israel into the regional economy.
But a faltering peace process since the May election of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has placed unexpected obstacles before the Cairo gathering.
Gulf Arab analysts say the conference, which starts on November 12, will bring into focus new hurdles to trading with Israel which have arisen since Netanyahu's election.

One Omani businessman spoke of a "new psychological block" to dealing with Israel after Netanyahu's election. Another said the seeds of better economic ties had been sown, but any further stalling of the peace process could delay investment and trade.

"I believe Omani companies see no future in doing business with Israelis until they see the peace process moving forward. Contacts right now are at a standstill because the Israeli side did not keep to their word," another Omani businessman said.
"They have shut their doors in front of us since the slowdown of peace talks," he added.

Some businessmen say the first steps to real business are being taken, but many shy away from publicising these, under pressure from their peers in the GCC and Arab League not to treat Israel as they would friendly states.
Since September's Palestinian-Israeli clashes over Israel's opening of a tunnel near Jerusalem's al-Aqsa mosque, Islam's third holiest site, Qatar has put contacts with Israel on hold.
But Qatari businessmen continue to pursue trade with Israel, a Qatar Chamber of Commerce and Industry official said.

"Offically, we distanced ourself as the chamber from the 18-businessmen's delegation which was to visit Tel Aviv last month. But if somebody wants to go as a private citizen, we have no objection," he told Reuters.
The mission was to explore joint ventures in agriculture, power, mineral water and petrochemicals.
"We know, despite the official stand, some businessmen still meet Israelis in Amman, Cairo and Jerusalem," he said.
